decision: read the 382-line PRD end to end, confirmed its arithmetic by hand
why: the whole build keys off the pricing convention in section 6, so a wrong formula would poison every screen
result: all 4 seeded yields and the worked example reproduce exactly

decision: started a real Postgres 16.13 locally instead of mocking the database
why: the hard requirements are atomic settlement and idempotency, and neither is testable against a fake
result: server up, psql connects

decision: found two dangling PRD cross-references
why: the PRD promises a five-minute runbook in section 19 and open decisions in section 16, but it stops at section 15
result: open, flagged to the user

decision: made base units a branded bigint instead of a number or a decimal library
why: javascript refuses to mix bigint and number, so a stray float in the money path stops compiling instead of silently rounding
result: 31 tests green

decision: put every rounding decision behind one mulDivRound helper
why: the PRD wants source-asset rounding stated on confirmation, and one convention beats re-deriving it per call site
result: XSGD conversion reconciles

decision: added largest-remainder pro-rata allocation for maturity payouts
why: rounding each holder separately leaves a few base units unpaid, which breaks the rule that holdings sum to outstanding face
result: parts sum to total exactly across 3 and 7 holders

decision: wrote the section 6 formulas once and tested against PRD literals, not against my own output
why: a demo shown to banks dies on a visibly wrong yield
result: worked example and all 4 seeded yields reproduce

decision: fixed formatUnits returning string in one branch and an object in the other
why: the union let me read .text off a string, which printed 320,458.undefined
result: caught by the XSGD test, now green

decision: corrected my own test rather than the code on the target-yield case
why: 244,632 is right for 8.9 percent; the PRD's 244,625 comes from the unrounded 8.911 percent
result: both figures now asserted

decision: put the section 7 lifecycle in one transition table keyed by event
why: the alternative is status checks sprinkled through every route, which is how an illegal transition slips in
result: 17 tests green, incl. maker-checker refusals

decision: derived maturity from the clock instead of storing it
why: advancing the demo clock must re-age every payable at once, and a stored flag would go stale
result: matures at 0 days, leaves settled and draft alone

decision: modelled supplier accept/reject as receipt state, not a lifecycle state
why: the PRD asks for the option in section 3 but its section 7 diagram has no state for it and never says what reject does
result: open, assumption recorded

decision: split the demo clock into a fixed T0 plus an offset
why: reset world becomes one assignment back to zero, and the PRD's relative seed dates keep their meaning
result: 20 tests green

decision: worked in UTC calendar days, never local time or instants
why: a payable matures on a date, and the booth laptop and tablet must agree regardless of their timezones
result: leap day and year boundary covered

decision: wrote docs/ASSUMPTIONS.md for every place the PRD ran out
why: the user is away, so a decision they would want to overrule has to be findable rather than buried in a diff
result: 8 entries, incl. the 2 dangling section refs

decision: built the design tokens around tables and tabular numerals, not cards
why: the PRD asks for the visual language of a treasury portal, where figures get compared down a column
result: shell renders, http 200

decision: put the no-real-funds ribbon in the root layout
why: section 11 requires it always visible, and a layout-level ribbon means no route can render without it
result: present in served html

decision: cleared both npm advisories by bumping vitest to 5
why: dev-only and the critical one needs the vitest UI server, but zero beats explaining why it is fine
result: 0 vulnerabilities, 68 tests still green

decision: derived the settled row as 312,900 over 90 days by search, not by guess
why: the PRD states a 9.2 percent realised yield but leaves the price and holding period to us
result: 9.202 percent, rounds to the stated 9.2

decision: ran candidate 2's schema against real postgres instead of just reading it
why: a schema that does not apply is a wish, and reading would not have caught either bug below
result: 2 defects found

decision: found: CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER cannot use REFERENCING NEW TABLE in postgres
why: constraint triggers must be FOR EACH ROW; the candidate used a statement-level transition table
result: fixed by making it FOR EACH ROW deferred, rest of schema then applies clean

decision: found: the conservation trigger rejects a legitimate mint
why: it groups a system account by its own name and the token leg by payable id, so a mint's two legs land in different dimensions and neither nets to zero
result: candidate 2's central mechanism is broken as written

decision: candidate 3 VERIFIED against real postgres: mint accepted, unbalanced entry refused
why: this is the check candidate 2 failed, so it is the one that actually separates the designs
result: holding 2500000000, 0 projection mismatches, money-from-nothing rejected

decision: candidate 3 treats each payable as an asset id, so conservation groups by one uniform dimension
why: that is precisely what candidate 2 got wrong by grouping system accounts under their own name
result: correct for both cash and token legs

decision: candidate 3 holds listed quantity in a wallet_listed escrow account
why: it makes 'listed quantity is locked to the listing' structural instead of a check every caller must remember
result: v_holding splits free_base from listed_base

decision: candidate 3 refuses a journal leg written outside ledger.post
why: project_leg raises unless the balance row was pre-created and locked, so the sanctioned path is the only path
result: my raw insert was correctly rejected

decision: candidate 1 VERIFIED: mint balances, double spend refused, proof function catches a real inconsistency
why: its central claims are structural, so they had to be executed rather than read
result: outstanding 2500000000 derived, -2500000001 rejected, verify_world flagged my hand-seeded status

decision: candidate 1 carries both legs in one movement row, so an unbalanced entry is unwritable
why: the other three check that legs net to zero; candidate 1 leaves nothing to check
result: no conservation trigger exists and none is needed

decision: candidate 1 has no outstanding_face column; it derives supply as the negated zero-address balance
why: that is ERC-1155 totalSupply, so there is no second copy of the number to drift
result: read back 2500000000 after mint

decision: confirmed the PRD's XSGD wording is consistent and my implementation matches
why: section 10's rate is XUSD per XSGD, so dividing by it multiplies by 1.31, same as section 6
result: 320,458.7500 XSGD, independently reproduced by a design runner

decision: confirmed BIGINT and SUM(bigint) both reach node-postgres as strings, not numbers
why: safe by default, but every read boundary has to parse to bigint and the hazard is someone reaching for Number()
result: string 2500000000 for both

decision: SUM(bigint) is numeric in postgres, not bigint
why: a view that sums base units silently changes the column type, which is where a float would first appear
result: must cast sums back to bigint in every view

decision: CORRECTION: my lean toward candidate 1 was wrong; the cross-judge caught a fatal defect I missed
why: I verified a mint and a direct UPDATE but never the ON CONFLICT path with a negative delta, which is the path every real operation takes
evidence: this row supersedes the earlier candidate 1 rows
result: candidate 1 rejected as base

decision: verified: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE cannot apply a negative delta under a non-negative CHECK
why: postgres validates the raw candidate row before resolving the conflict, so 1000 + (-400) never runs
result: wallet stuck at 2500000000, no debit can commit

decision: BASE CHOSEN: candidate 3
why: it is the only design that survived execution unmodified, and it sidesteps the ON CONFLICT trap by pre-creating balance rows at zero and mutating via AFTER INSERT UPDATE
evidence: cross-judge scores plus my own mint and money-from-nothing tests
result: mint, unbalanced rejection and partial transfer all hold

decision: candidate 3's earlier refusal of my raw insert was the design working, not a defect
why: project_leg demands a pre-created locked balance row, which is exactly what avoids the ON CONFLICT trap
result: understood in hindsight

decision: implemented ledger.post, the single write surface, and drove the whole runbook through it
why: the base design shipped this function as pseudocode, so it was the one piece nothing could be built on until it existed
result: issue to settle passes with every PRD figure asserted

decision: replaced the journal immutability RULE with a BEFORE UPDATE trigger
why: postgres refuses INSERT ON CONFLICT on any table carrying an update rule, which would have cost the idempotency gate
result: gate works, immutability kept, and it now raises instead of silently discarding

decision: moved listing and bid FKs off the idempotency gate insert
why: publish_listing and place_bid create the very rows the FK points at, so the gate cannot reference them yet
result: FK violation gone

decision: escrow verified: publishing a listing moves quantity out of free into wallet_listed
why: the judge flagged this as untested in the base design
result: free 0, listed 2500000000

decision: proved the contended accept with two real connections, not by reasoning
why: duplicate acceptance is the PRD's worst-case failure and the one thing a single-session test cannot show
result: loser blocked then got 'listing is filled'; exactly 1 trade, books balanced

decision: 13 invariant checks each try the forbidden thing and assert nothing moved
why: a refusal that still shifted a balance would be worse than no refusal
result: all held, incl. partial sale and split settlement

decision: made the section 12 no-floats scan a real CI stage instead of a comment
why: the schema shipped it as prose, and prose does not fail a build
result: 0 float or numeric columns in the money path

decision: one command runs unit, typecheck, schema scan, runbook, invariants and concurrency
why: the user is away, so the next person needs one thing to run, not six
result: all green

decision: registered pg type parsers so BIGINT and SUM both arrive as bigint
why: otherwise money reaches javascript as a string and the first contributor needing arithmetic reaches for Number()
result: integration test asserts typeof bigint on a column and an aggregate

decision: post() returns a tagged union instead of throwing
why: every caller is a server action that has to render a refusal inline, and an exception loses the reason
result: 9 integration tests green

decision: moved the funds-vs-quantity distinction into post_legs where the asset kind is known
why: one CHECK guards every asset, so the constraint name alone cannot tell an overdraft from an over-quantity move
result: caught by my own integration test expecting the wrong code

decision: pinned the pool to one connection per instance with lock and statement timeouts
why: vercel scales instances out, so a big per-instance pool multiplies into a connection limit failure
result: open

decision: seeded the past by living through it rather than writing ledger rows by hand
why: the settled and overdue rows need real histories, and hand-written rows would have to be made to reconcile by luck
result: world lands on 2026-10-01, books prove themselves

decision: extended post() so a series listing is just a listing with twelve legs
why: the PRD requires a seeded series, and a second code path for lots would be where the escrow invariant drifts
result: 12 members, one holder, lists at 99.20

decision: added app.erp_invoice for the SAP-style import picker
why: the PRD asks for ten pre-generated sample invoices and the base schema had nowhere to put them
result: 10 seeded, incl. the runbook's 250,000 over 90 days

decision: split db.sh reset from db.sh bare
why: the seed and the fixture-bearing tests both want to own the singleton world row
result: all stages green side by side

decision: one read function per screen, each taking the clock
why: nothing time-derived is stored, so a screen that cached a tenor would be wrong the moment someone fast-forwarded
result: 27 tests green, PRD yields reproduce through the full stack

decision: applied the clock-to-status derivation in exactly one place
why: two screens disagreeing about whether a payable is overdue is the kind of thing an audience notices
result: stored issued, displayed overdue, 45 days past due

decision: gave each vitest file its own database
why: vitest runs files in parallel and both were resetting the same one, which is a race waiting to be flaky
result: 106 tests green twice running

decision: built all 16 screens plus the demo controls bar and persona switcher
why: the PRD names each screen and its contents, so the check is coverage against that list
result: every screen renders, checked in a real browser

decision: changed ActionButton to take a server action plus args instead of a closure
why: a server component cannot hand a closure to a client component, so two screens 500'd while the client-rendered ones worked
result: 16 of 16 now render

decision: wrote scripts/screens.mjs to walk every screen as every persona in a real browser
why: a build says nothing about whether a page renders, and this caught the two that did not
result: found the closure bug that typecheck and build both passed

decision: wrote scripts/serve.sh after building over a running server served a stale route table
why: doing it by hand is three commands in an order that matters, which is exactly what a script is for
result: no more phantom 404s

decision: drove the whole runbook through the real UI, click by click, as five personas
why: the PRD's headline criterion is that a viewer can do this, which no SQL test can show
result: 18 steps, ERP import to settlement, 23s

decision: found a type mismatch that every SQL test passed over
why: COALESCE mixed json text with the credit_grade enum, and the SQL fixtures all started from an already-certified payable
result: fixed, and tests/ledger/lifecycle.sql now walks the whole approval path

decision: pinned the runbook to the created reference instead of a page position
why: the marketplace sorts by yield, so 'the last listing' was the cheapest one, not the new one
result: bid landed on the wrong payable until fixed

decision: made Reset world execute the SQL files directly instead of shelling out to psql
why: vercel has no shell, no psql and no scripts directory, so the control would have failed only in production
result: verified through the UI: clock back to T0, listings and yields restored

decision: stripped psql meta-commands and traced the SQL files into the deployment
why: a backslash directive is fine through psql and a syntax error through the driver, which is how the first attempt failed
result: 0 server errors on reset

decision: CORRECTION: ASSUMPTIONS.md claimed supplier accept/reject was built when only a hardcoded 'accepted' existed
why: auditing the log against the code found my own documentation overstating what shipped
evidence: this row supersedes the earlier lifecycle receipt row
result: built it properly rather than downgrading the claim

decision: added receipt_status with an inbox, and gated listing and transfer on acceptance
why: PRD section 3 question 7 makes it one of the questions the demo must answer, and section 8 calls screen 6 an inbox
result: runbook is now 19 steps incl. taking delivery

decision: declining returns the quantity to the anchor rather than burning it
why: burning would break the rule that holdings sum to outstanding face, and cancellation is out of scope so there is no state to move to
result: face intact after a decline, verified

decision: added the Trigger overdue control and its recovery screen
why: section 11 lists five demo controls and only four were built
result: 17 screens render

decision: SETTLED by the user: direct purchase only, no lending pool, ever
why: this was the one open assumption that was not a cheap reversal, and it is now closed
result: removing the caveat from ASSUMPTIONS.md and the PRD

decision: user: section 19 was left in the PRD by mistake; remove the references
why: the runbook I wrote from the rest of the PRD stands on its own
result: editing the PRD

decision: user: the demo runs from late October and then indefinitely, on a public URL
why: a world hardcoded to a fixed T0 looks stale the moment it is demoed months later
result: making T0 the seed date, not a constant

decision: user: anyone can use the URL; only admin resets; seed data must be realistic and plentiful
why: a public demo is judged on whether the data looks like a real programme
result: expanding the seed and gating reset

decision: made T0 the day the world was seeded instead of a fixed date
why: the demo runs on a public URL indefinitely, and a fixed T0 makes every tenor look short within weeks
result: T0 = today, verified after reset

decision: expanded the seed from 6 payables to 29, across all three grades and 30 to 180 days
why: a public demo is judged on whether the data looks like a real programme rather than a fixture
result: 26 entities, 15 users, 9 open listings, 24 ERP invoices, 115 events

decision: seeded two payables sold in part, so a split holding exists on arrival
why: the PRD's partial-quantity story needs a payable with two current holders to point at
result: 2 holders each

decision: seeded 24 ERP invoices rather than the PRD's 10
why: every visitor to a public URL who issues a payable consumes one, and a picker that empties is a worse demo
result: test relaxed to at least 10

decision: gave buy-now the same settlement branch as accept_bid rather than its own
why: two places that move money is exactly what this ledger design exists to avoid; buy-now is an acceptance against a price published in advance
result: 6 new invariants pass, including that a replay pays once

decision: refused a seller buying their own listing, at the ledger
why: the trade nets to nothing but still marks the listing filled, quietly retiring a lot that never changed hands
result: tests/ledger/invariants.sql section 9

decision: gave the buy-now box its own debit line, balance and shortfall check
why: it inherited the bid form's check, which prices a different number; a lender would have confirmed to find out they could not afford it
result: funding asset lifted above both paths, since it prices both

decision: gated Reset behind the admin persona, a typed RESET, and an optional ADATA_RESET_PIN
why: the URL is public and a reset lands on every connected session; the persona switcher is open by design, so only the PIN is a real lock and the screen says so when none is set
result: runbook steps 22-24 prove all three in the browser

decision: filtered the marketplace in TypeScript rather than SQL
why: tenor, yield and the maturity cutoff are derived from the demo clock and the §6 formulas; pushing them into SQL means a second yield implementation that has to agree with the first forever
result: 19 unit tests, no database needed

decision: put the filter in the URL instead of component state
why: a narrowed marketplace becomes a link the presenter can send, and the back button undoes a filter
result: runbook step 13 asserts the URL carries grade=AAA

decision: made the headline figures describe the filtered view, not the whole book
why: a lender who narrowed to 30-day AAA wants the best yield among those; the unfiltered number answers a question nobody asked
result: Open lots becomes 'Lots matching, of N open'

decision: expanded a series with <details> rather than a client component
why: the twelve rows are already on the page, so expanding costs no round trip and needs no JavaScript; collapsed by default because the members are a detail, not the headline
result: runbook step 15 expands all 12

decision: a series detail screen was showing the whole world's event history
why: readEvents had no series filter, so the fallback was every event in the world; a lender reading a series lot saw unrelated trades as if they were its history
result: now 25 rows, all of them the 12 issuances, 12 acceptances and the listing

decision: showed the holder against every member invoice
why: PRD 13 requires each member wholly held by one wallet; a per-row holder makes the rule visible instead of asserted
result: footer states whether one wallet holds them all

decision: put manual entry and ERP import through one create_payable branch
why: the difference is only where four facts come from; two branches would be two places that insert a payable and two audit shapes
result: the approval queue cannot tell them apart

decision: added a unique index on (supplier, invoice reference)
why: manual entry lets a preparer type an invoice number by hand, and financing one invoice twice is the fraud this programme exists to prevent
result: refused with its own message, proven in the browser

decision: a duplicate invoice reported 'that persona cannot take this action'
why: every form refusal was folded into ADA15/ADA19, so a preparer who mistyped an invoice number was told they lacked permission; found by driving the form, not by reading it
result: each refusal now says what is wrong and what to do

decision: made user removal a deactivation, not a delete
why: every journal entry names its actor, and PRD 10 requires a receipt reopened from history to match the one shown at confirmation
result: tests assert no entry loses its actor

decision: refused removing the last account of an organisation
why: a wallet is reached through its users, so the last removal would leave holdings on the books with nobody able to act on them
result: seed gives four organisations a second account so the control is demonstrable

decision: manual entry offered twelve suppliers who could never accept a payable
why: they sold everything into the series and have no live account; a payable issued to one would strand at issuance waiting for a receipt nobody could give
evidence: ADA31 plus a filtered supplier list
result: the ERP path was never exposed to this, its register only names onboarded suppliers

decision: all six PRD gaps built and verified end to end
why: the user asked for all of them; each is proven in the browser rather than by reading the code
result: 9 suites green, 20 screen-persona pairs render, 33 runbook steps in 45s

decision: proved the supplier-to-lender buy-now round trip, not just a seeded price
why: the README claimed a supplier can set a buy-now price; only the seeded values were ever exercised, so the claim outran the proof
result: what the supplier types is what the lender is offered

decision: the programme limit was stored and displayed but enforced nowhere
why: a number on a screen that no code consults invites a viewer to believe a control exists; the issuer certification status was equally decorative
result: 11 assertions including the exact-boundary case

decision: capped outstanding face rather than cumulative issuance
why: the certification screen already said currently outstanding and headroom; a cumulative cap means a programme that eventually stops working however promptly it pays
result: settling frees headroom, asserted

decision: the limit progress bar was a second element answering to programme limit
why: its aria-label shadowed the new input, so a screen reader and Playwright both found two; the bar is redundant to the stat above it
result: found by the browser check failing on a strict-mode violation

decision: institutional eligibility was a UI notice, not a rule
why: PRD 9 says only institutional lender accounts can bid or buy; the ledger accepted a bid from a supplier or from ADATA itself
result: checked at place_bid and again at settlement, since an account can be removed between the two

decision: swept for other rules the screens knew and the ledger did not
why: the programme limit turned out to be decorative, so the same question was worth asking of every other stated rule
result: 3 found and fixed; 1 confirmed transitively enforced and commented rather than duplicated

decision: resumed from the PR 2 handover and this decision log, not from a transcript
why: the only transcript in this workspace is this session's own, and the handover was written for whoever picks this up
result: one buildable item left: the funding-asset picker at settlement

decision: checked the handover's four pointers against the code before building on them
why: a passing self-report is not proof, and the line numbers had to survive the commit that landed after the description was written
result: all four hold: settle branch hardcodes XUSD, no picker, key omits the asset

decision: left deploying and the presenter dry run to the user
why: both need things this session does not have, Neon and Vercel credentials and a person to walk the script
result: open

decision: ran the whole suite on the untouched merge commit before changing anything
why: every later check has to measure against a real baseline, and a fresh container is a new machine
